summary: This informational document describes the common practice of listening on TCP port 6697 for incoming IRC connections encrypted with TLS/SSL.

eli5.summary: Chat servers have a usual door number for private chats. This writes down that the number is 6697.

subtitle: Writes down the common practice of running encrypted IRC on TCP port 6697.

tldr.problem: Registered ports for IRC exist, but IRC networks do not use them, so users had no well-known port for encrypted IRC and might not know their network supported it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC records the community consensus: IRC servers listen on TCP port 6697 for connections that start with a normal TLS/SSL handshake, and IANA assigned the port under the service name ircs-u.
tldr.outcome: It only describes client-to-server encryption. Server links, malicious operators, compromised servers and clients are outside what it protects against.

today: RFC 7194 is an Informational, Independent Submission that updates RFC 1459 and has not been obsoleted or updated itself. It documents port 6697 as the assigned port for IRC over TLS/SSL.

sections.title: Why a Common Port Was Needed
sections.content:
System port assignments already exist for IRC: TCP/UDP port 194 for plain text and TCP/UDP port 994 for TLS/SSL encrypted traffic. The RFC says IRC networks commonly do not use them, for reasons of convenience and general availability on systems where no root access is granted or desired.

Instead, IRC networks have long defaulted to TCP port 6667 for plain text, which falls inside the IRCU assignment of TCP/UDP ports 6665-6669. The IRC community reached a similar consensus about TCP port 6697 for IRC encrypted with TLS/SSL, and this RFC records that practice.
sections.eli5: There were official door numbers for chat, but nobody used them because they were awkward. People settled on their own numbers instead, and this document writes down the one for private chats.

sections.title: How a TLS Connection Starts
sections.content:
An IRC client connects to an IRC server. Right after that, a normal TLS/SSL handshake takes place. Once the TLS/SSL connection is established, a normal IRC connection is set up through the tunnel. There is no special IRC-level negotiation to switch encryption on.

Two optional extras are mentioned. The server may set a specific user mode (umode) marking the client as using TLS/SSL, and a server may let users create channels that only clients connected via TLS/SSL can join.

The RFC points to RFC 1459, RFC 2810, RFC 2811, RFC 2812 and RFC 2813 for how IRC itself works, and warns that IRC is extremely fragmented. Most implementations treat the later RFCs as suggestions, not as binding.
sections.eli5: You knock on the private door, you and the server first agree on a secret code, and only then do you start chatting. Some servers also put a little badge on you to show you came in the private way.

sections.title: Certificate Details
sections.content:
The server's certificate should be issued by a commonly trusted certification authority (CA). Its Common Name should match the server's fully qualified domain name (FQDN) or use appropriate wildcards, and the client should verify the certificate.

If a client also uses a certificate, it should come from a commonly trusted CA or one designated by the IRC network. Its Common Name should match the main IRC nickname, or the registered nick or account name where the network offers nick registration or grouped nicks. Where nick registration exists, the client certificate should be used to identify the user against the nick database.

All of these are should in lower case; the RFC does not use RFC 2119 keywords.
sections.eli5: The server shows an ID card from someone everybody trusts, and your app checks it. If you have your own ID card, it should carry your chat nickname.

sections.title: What This Does and Does Not Protect
sections.content:
Without a well-established port for IRC over TLS/SSL, users may not realize their network supports encryption and so may not use it even if they wanted to.

The document describes only client-to-server encryption. It lists threats that this cannot address: malicious administrators, compromised servers, insecure server-to-server communication, channels that do not enforce encryption for all members, malicious clients, and compromised client machines where logs are stored. Users who fear these need additional safeguards.

Server links are out of scope because there are no commonly accepted ports or back-end protocols; these are normally set by bilateral agreement. All operators are encouraged to use strong encryption for back-end traffic.
sections.eli5: A private door keeps people in the hallway from listening. It does not help if the person you are chatting with, or the room itself, is not trustworthy.

sections.title: The IANA Port Assignment
sections.content:
IANA assigned TCP port 6697 for IRC via TLS/SSL, with the service name ircs-u and the description "Internet Relay Chat via TLS/SSL".

Appendix A adds supporting data: as of October 2010, ten of the top twenty IRC networks supported TLS/SSL. Only one of those did not support it on port 6697 and had no plans to. All the others supported it already or did so after being contacted by the author.
sections.eli5: The official list of door numbers now has an entry saying that 6697 is the private chat door.
